title: Security is a form of care
excerpt: Security awareness is not about fear or showing what you can access. It is the discipline of reducing risk, respecting consent, protecting privacy, using privilege responsibly, and making safe behavior easier.

sections.label: Principle
sections.title: Security knowledge creates responsibility, not entitlement.
paragraphs: Technical ability is not authorization. Knowing how to access, inspect, recover, test, or secure an account does not create permission to do so.
Good security work begins with scope, consent, necessity, and accountability. The goal is to reduce exposure without creating a new privacy violation in the process.

Even when the intention is protective, accessing another person's account, private messages, files, location, credentials, or devices without clear authorization can cause harm, destroy trust, and cross legal or ethical boundaries.
sections.callout: The safest rule is simple: if access is not yours, obtain explicit authorization before using it.

sections.label: Mindset
sections.title: Security is risk management, not paranoia.
paragraphs: Security is the process of identifying what matters, understanding realistic threats, reducing unnecessary exposure, detecting abnormal behavior, and recovering when controls fail.

Perfect security does not exist. Strong security uses layers so that one mistake, one stolen password, one vulnerable application, or one compromised device does not automatically become a total compromise.
points: Protect what matters most first
Reduce attack surface before adding complexity
Assume individual controls can fail
Prefer layered safeguards over a single defensive measure
Design for detection, containment, and recovery as well as prevention
Reassess risk when technology, people, privileges, or circumstances change

sections.label: Threat modeling
sections.title: Know what you are protecting and from whom.
paragraphs: A threat model prevents security from becoming a collection of random precautions. Start with assets, identities, trust relationships, data flows, likely adversaries, failure modes, and the consequences of compromise.

The appropriate controls for a public social account are different from those for an administrator account, financial account, production server, password manager, source-code repository, or device containing sensitive personal data.
points: Assets: accounts, devices, credentials, data, reputation, money, infrastructure
Threats: credential theft, malware, impersonation, fraud, stalking, insider misuse, data leakage, service disruption
Exposure: public information, reused credentials, old sessions, third-party applications, unnecessary services
Impact: privacy loss, financial loss, account takeover, operational disruption, identity abuse
Controls: authentication, authorization, segmentation, logging, encryption, backups, recovery procedures

sections.label: Identity
sections.title: Protect identity before protecting everything behind it.
paragraphs: Most online systems ultimately trust an identity. If an attacker controls the identity provider, email account, recovery method, password manager, or primary device, many downstream protections can be bypassed.
Prioritize the accounts that can reset other accounts. Recovery channels should be treated as privileged security infrastructure.
points: Use a unique password for every important account
Use a reputable password manager instead of memorizing or reusing passwords
Enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible
Prefer phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys or hardware security keys for high-value accounts
Protect primary email accounts more strongly than ordinary accounts
Review recovery email addresses, recovery phone numbers, and trusted devices
Remove obsolete sessions, devices, application passwords, and third-party integrations
Store backup codes securely and separately from the device they protect

sections.label: Authentication
sections.title: Authentication should resist both guessing and deception.
paragraphs: Passwords alone are vulnerable to reuse, phishing, credential stuffing, malware, and social engineering. Strong authentication combines independent safeguards and gives users a reliable way to recognize unexpected activity.
Authentication factors are only useful when recovery mechanisms are protected with equal care.
points: Use unique, high-entropy passwords
Prefer passkeys or hardware-backed authentication where available
Avoid SMS as the strongest available factor when stronger options exist
Never approve an authentication request you did not initiate
Treat unexpected verification codes as an indication that someone may be attempting access
Review recent sign-ins after suspicious authentication activity
Secure recovery channels against takeover
Remove obsolete authenticators and trusted devices

sections.label: Privilege
sections.title: Privileged access should be rare, temporary, and visible.
paragraphs: Administrator, root, sudo, cloud-owner, domain-admin, database-admin, repository-admin, network-admin, backup-admin, and security-console access can affect systems far beyond an ordinary user account. That power should be deliberately constrained.
Privilege should be granted because a task requires it, not because it is convenient. Sensitive actions should be attributable to a specific identity and reviewable afterward.
Possessing administrator credentials does not mean every technically available action is authorized.
points: Apply least privilege: grant only the permissions required for the task
Separate daily-use accounts from administrative accounts
Avoid shared administrator credentials
Use named identities so actions are attributable
Use time-limited or just-in-time privilege where supported
Require stronger authentication for privileged identities
Log privileged access and important administrative actions
Review privileged group membership regularly
Remove access immediately when responsibilities change
Use separate privileged accounts for infrastructure, cloud, databases, and security tooling where appropriate
Never use privileged access to browse private information unrelated to the authorized task
Treat secrets, tokens, API keys, SSH keys, recovery codes, and signing keys as privileged credentials
sections.callout: Privilege is a capability to perform an authorized task, not permission to inspect everything the capability can reach.

sections.label: Privileged identities
sections.title: High-impact accounts deserve stronger controls.
paragraphs: Some identities can change authentication policies, create accounts, disable monitoring, modify backups, alter network access, deploy code, or access large amounts of data. These accounts should be treated as critical infrastructure.
points: Protect root and superuser credentials separately
Use dedicated cloud-administrator identities
Protect domain and directory administrators
Restrict hypervisor and virtualization management access
Secure database administrative accounts
Protect backup and disaster-recovery administration
Restrict security-tool and logging-platform administrators
Monitor privilege escalation events
Use break-glass accounts only for emergencies
Alert when emergency accounts are used

sections.label: Separation of duties
sections.title: No single identity should control every critical step.
paragraphs: Separation of duties reduces the consequences of compromised credentials, accidental mistakes, and insider misuse. Critical actions can require multiple roles, approvals, or independent verification.
points: Separate account creation from privilege approval
Separate development from production administration where appropriate
Separate payment initiation from approval
Separate security monitoring from routine system administration when practical
Use independent approval for highly sensitive configuration changes
Avoid giving one service account unnecessary access across multiple trust boundaries

sections.label: Consent
sections.title: Helping is not the same as having permission.
paragraphs: Concern for someone's security can justify warning them, explaining a weakness, or helping them review settings. It does not automatically authorize account access, private-data inspection, password use, device access, tracking, or impersonation.
Security work should be performed with the owner's knowledge unless a clearly established professional, organizational, or legal authorization already exists.
points: Explain what access is required before requesting it
Explain what information might become visible during the work
Define what changes will be made
Use the minimum access required
Stop when the authorized task is complete
Remove temporary access afterward
Do not reuse credentials obtained for one purpose for another purpose
When possible, let the account owner perform sensitive steps themselves
sections.callout: Security knowledge should reduce another person's exposure, not become another source of exposure.

sections.label: Privacy
sections.title: Privacy is part of security, not a separate concern.
paragraphs: A system can be technically secure and still expose far more information than necessary. Privacy asks whether data should be collected, retained, linked, shared, or visible in the first place.
Minimizing data reduces both the consequences of compromise and the opportunities for misuse.
points: Collect only data that has a defined purpose
Limit who can see sensitive information
Reduce public exposure of phone numbers, email addresses, location, routines, and personal identifiers
Review social-media visibility, tagging, contact discovery, and location settings
Avoid publishing information that can assist account recovery attacks or impersonation
Use separate identities or contact addresses when separation materially reduces risk
Delete unnecessary copies of sensitive data when retention is no longer required
Encrypt sensitive data in transit and, where appropriate, at rest
Do not expose private information merely to prove that a vulnerability exists

sections.label: Data minimization
sections.title: The safest sensitive data is often the data you never collected.
paragraphs: Every additional copy, export, backup, log entry, screenshot, integration, and database field creates another place where sensitive information can leak.
Data minimization should apply to production systems, testing environments, support systems, analytics platforms, logs, and human workflows.
points: Avoid collecting fields that have no operational purpose
Use synthetic or anonymized data for testing where possible
Redact secrets and personal data from support tickets
Avoid copying production databases into insecure development environments
Limit bulk exports
Review public sharing links
Set retention limits
Delete expired or unnecessary datasets

sections.label: Human attacks
sections.title: Social engineering attacks trust before technology.
paragraphs: Attackers often bypass technical controls by creating urgency, authority, fear, curiosity, sympathy, familiarity, or confusion.

A message does not become trustworthy because it contains personal information. That information may have been collected from public sources, previous breaches, another compromised account, or data brokers.
Verification should move to a trusted channel rather than continuing inside the suspicious interaction.
points: Do not approve unexpected authentication prompts
Do not disclose one-time codes, backup codes, passwords, or recovery keys
Verify unusual money, credential, or access requests through a separate trusted channel
Inspect sender identity and destination before entering credentials
Be cautious with unexpected attachments, shared documents, QR codes, shortened links, and login pages
Treat urgency as a reason to verify, not a reason to bypass procedure
Remember that executives, friends, relatives, support staff, administrators, and service providers can all be impersonated

sections.label: Phishing
sections.title: The objective of phishing is usually trust, credentials, or execution.
paragraphs: Phishing can arrive through email, text messages, social media, collaboration platforms, QR codes, fake login pages, telephone calls, or compromised trusted accounts.
The safest response is to independently navigate to the real service rather than following the path provided by the suspicious message.
points: Navigate directly to important services instead of using suspicious login links
Verify unexpected file-sharing invitations
Check the actual domain, not only the displayed brand name
Be cautious when a login page appears after opening a document
Report suspicious messages
Do not assume a message is safe because antivirus software did not block it

sections.label: MFA fatigue
sections.title: Repeated authentication prompts can be an attack.
paragraphs: Attackers with a stolen password may repeatedly trigger multi-factor prompts hoping the user eventually approves one. This is sometimes called MFA fatigue or push bombing.
points: Reject authentication requests you did not initiate
Change the affected password if unexplained prompts continue
Review active sessions
Notify the security team in managed environments
Prefer number matching, passkeys, hardware keys, or other phishing-resistant mechanisms where available

sections.label: Devices
sections.title: A trusted account on an untrusted device is still exposed.
paragraphs: Endpoints frequently hold active sessions, saved credentials, browser cookies, private files, authentication applications, and access to other systems. Device security therefore protects far more than the device itself.
points: Install security updates promptly
Keep browsers, applications, firmware, and operating systems supported
Use screen locking and device encryption
Use a strong local authentication method
Do not disable security controls merely to remove an inconvenience
Install software from trusted sources
Remove unused applications
Review application permissions
Avoid routine work from administrator or root sessions
Protect lost-device recovery and remote-wipe capabilities
Treat unexpected remote-access software as a high-risk finding

sections.label: Mobile security
sections.title: Phones are identity devices, not just communication devices.
paragraphs: A mobile device often contains email, authenticator applications, password managers, financial applications, messaging, location history, photographs, and account-recovery capabilities.
points: Use a strong screen lock
Enable device encryption
Keep the operating system updated
Restrict lock-screen notification content when privacy matters
Review application permissions
Protect SIM and carrier accounts
Avoid installing applications from unknown sources
Enable lost-device location and remote wipe where appropriate
Remove old trusted devices from important accounts

sections.label: Browser security
sections.title: The browser is often the gateway to everything else.
paragraphs: Modern browsers hold active sessions, saved passwords, extensions, cookies, payment information, and authenticated access to cloud services.
points: Keep the browser updated
Remove unused extensions
Review extension permissions
Use separate browser profiles where identity separation matters
Do not ignore certificate or connection warnings
Log out of sensitive services on shared systems
Review remembered devices and persistent sessions

sections.label: Networks
sections.title: Reduce unnecessary trust on networks.
paragraphs: Being connected to the same network should not automatically imply permission to reach every service. Internal networks, home networks, cloud networks, and management networks all benefit from limiting unnecessary paths.
points: Expose only services that must be reachable
Use firewalls and network segmentation to limit lateral movement
Separate management interfaces from public-facing services where practical
Use encrypted protocols instead of plaintext equivalents
Change default credentials
Disable unused management services
Treat public Wi-Fi as untrusted
Secure routers, access points, DNS settings, and administrative interfaces
Inventory internet-facing services and remove forgotten exposure

sections.label: Remote access
sections.title: Remote administration is privileged access.
paragraphs: Remote desktop, SSH, VPN, remote-management platforms, web administration, and cloud consoles should be treated as high-value access paths.
points: Require strong authentication
Restrict source networks where practical
Avoid directly exposing management ports to the public internet
Monitor remote login activity
Disable obsolete remote-access services
Remove vendor or contractor access after work is complete
Use dedicated administrative pathways for critical infrastructure

sections.label: Applications
sections.title: Secure software should fail safely.
paragraphs: Applications should not depend on users making perfect security decisions. Secure defaults, explicit authorization checks, bounded sessions, safe error handling, input validation, dependency maintenance, and auditable security events reduce the amount of vigilance required from users.
points: Validate authorization on the server, not only in the interface
Protect sessions against theft, fixation, and excessive lifetime
Do not place secrets in source code, client-side files, logs, or public repositories
Validate and constrain untrusted input
Use maintained dependencies
Remove unused packages
Rate-limit sensitive operations where abuse is foreseeable
Design password reset and account recovery as security-critical flows
Log meaningful security events without logging unnecessary secrets
Provide safe defaults and understandable warnings
Assume ordinary users will make ordinary mistakes

sections.label: Authorization
sections.title: Authentication answers who you are. Authorization answers what you may do.
paragraphs: A valid login should never be treated as permission to access every resource. Applications must check whether the authenticated identity is authorized for each protected operation.
points: Enforce authorization on the server side
Check resource ownership
Use role-based or attribute-based access controls where appropriate
Deny access by default
Avoid trusting hidden interface elements as security controls
Test access boundaries between user roles
Review administrative APIs separately from ordinary user APIs

sections.label: Secrets
sections.title: Credentials should be difficult to steal and easy to revoke.
paragraphs: Passwords are only one kind of credential. API keys, access tokens, session cookies, SSH keys, private keys, certificates, recovery codes, database passwords, and cloud credentials may provide equal or greater access.
points: Never commit live secrets to public source control
Use secret-management systems or protected environment configuration
Rotate exposed credentials instead of merely deleting the visible copy
Scope tokens to the minimum permissions required
Give credentials the shortest practical lifetime
Use separate credentials for development, testing, and production
Protect private signing and encryption keys more strongly than ordinary data
Maintain an inventory of high-impact credentials and their owners

sections.label: Source control
sections.title: Repositories are part of the security boundary.
paragraphs: Source repositories may contain production logic, deployment workflows, infrastructure definitions, security configurations, issue discussions, and secrets accidentally committed in the past.
points: Protect maintainer and administrator accounts with strong MFA
Use branch protections for important branches
Restrict who can modify deployment workflows
Review third-party actions and automation
Scan for accidentally committed secrets
Rotate any exposed secret even after removing it from Git history
Review repository collaborators regularly
Limit deploy keys and automation tokens

sections.label: Dependencies
sections.title: Every dependency extends your trust boundary.
paragraphs: Libraries, packages, browser extensions, build tools, plugins, CI actions, container images, and vendor services can introduce vulnerabilities or become compromised.
points: Use maintained dependencies
Remove unused dependencies
Pin versions where appropriate
Review significant dependency changes
Monitor vulnerability advisories
Protect package-publishing accounts
Restrict build-system credentials
Prefer reputable sources for software packages

sections.label: Cloud security
sections.title: Cloud convenience does not remove access-control responsibility.
paragraphs: Cloud environments combine identity, infrastructure, networking, storage, secrets, logging, billing, and deployment controls. Misconfigured permissions can expose large amounts of data very quickly.
points: Protect root or owner accounts strongly
Use separate administrator identities
Avoid permanent broad access keys
Review public storage exposure
Enable audit logging
Restrict security-group and firewall rules
Use managed identity mechanisms where possible
Remove stale users, service accounts, keys, and roles
Monitor privilege changes

sections.label: Backups
sections.title: Recovery is a security control.
paragraphs: Backups matter only if they can be restored. Ransomware, accidental deletion, device failure, malicious insiders, account lockout, and configuration mistakes can all make recovery necessary.
A recovery plan should assume that the primary system, credentials, or normal communication channel may be unavailable.
points: Keep multiple copies of important data
Maintain at least one backup isolated from ordinary user access when practical
Protect backup credentials and administration separately
Test restores instead of assuming backups work
Document critical recovery dependencies
Preserve recovery codes and ownership evidence for essential accounts
Define who can authorize destructive restoration or failover actions

sections.label: Logging
sections.title: Logs provide accountability, but logs are sensitive too.
paragraphs: Security logs can reveal usernames, IP addresses, infrastructure details, access patterns, device information, locations, and sometimes personal data. They should be useful enough for investigation without becoming an unnecessary privacy archive.
points: Log authentication events
Log privilege changes
Log important configuration changes
Protect logs against unauthorized modification
Restrict access to logs
Avoid logging passwords, tokens, or secrets
Synchronize system clocks
Define retention periods
Monitor attempts to disable logging

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.title: You cannot respond to what you cannot see.
paragraphs: Monitoring should focus on events that help distinguish normal operation from compromise. More alerts are not automatically better; useful signals must be prioritized and investigated.
Security visibility should remain proportional to the defensive purpose. Monitoring is not permission for unnecessary surveillance.
points: Monitor authentication failures and unusual successful logins
Monitor administrator logins
Record security-setting changes
Alert on creation of unexpected privileged users
Detect new access tokens, SSH keys, forwarding rules, or persistence mechanisms
Track changes to critical configurations
Protect monitoring systems from the identities they monitor where practical
Define escalation paths before an incident occurs

sections.label: Warning signs
sections.title: Recognize common indicators of compromise.
points: Unexpected password-reset messages
Unexpected MFA prompts
Login alerts from unknown devices or locations
New recovery addresses or phone numbers
Unknown email forwarding rules
Unknown browser extensions
Unrecognized OAuth applications
Unexpected API tokens or SSH keys
New administrator accounts
Security controls disabled without explanation
Unusual outbound traffic
Files unexpectedly encrypted, deleted, renamed, or transferred
Sudden changes to permissions
Unknown remote-access software
Unexpected persistence after passwords are changed

sections.label: Incident response
sections.title: Contain first, preserve evidence, then recover deliberately.
paragraphs: When compromise is suspected, impulsive actions can destroy evidence or warn an attacker before containment is ready. Response should follow a defined process appropriate to the severity of the incident.

For personal accounts, the priorities are usually regaining trustworthy control, invalidating unauthorized access, securing recovery channels, checking connected accounts, and documenting what changed.
points: Confirm what is known and separate evidence from assumptions
Use a trusted device for recovery when the original device may be compromised
Revoke suspicious sessions
Revoke suspicious tokens and keys
Reset credentials from a trusted environment
Secure the primary email and recovery channels
Review forwarding rules, filters, trusted devices, recovery contacts, and MFA methods
Preserve relevant logs, alerts, timestamps, and notifications
Notify affected people or administrators when their action is required
Document remediation
Verify that the attacker no longer has a path back in

sections.label: Account compromise
sections.title: Recovery must close the attacker's return path.
paragraphs: Changing a password alone may not remove an attacker. Active sessions, OAuth grants, email forwarding rules, recovery changes, API tokens, application passwords, SSH keys, and newly created users may survive the password reset.
points: Change the password
Sign out other sessions
Review MFA methods
Review recovery contacts
Remove suspicious connected applications
Remove unknown API tokens
Remove unknown application passwords
Review email rules and forwarding
Review privileged users
Check connected accounts for follow-on compromise

sections.label: Malware awareness
sections.title: Assume compromise can persist beyond a single stolen password.
paragraphs: Credential-stealing malware, remote-access tools, malicious extensions, and infostealers can capture sessions and credentials repeatedly. If a device itself is compromised, account recovery from that same device may immediately expose the new credentials.
points: Use a trusted device for important recovery
Update the operating system and security tools
Investigate unexpected software
Review startup and persistence mechanisms through trusted tools
Remove suspicious browser extensions
Rotate important credentials after the device is trusted again
Consider rebuilding heavily compromised systems rather than relying on incomplete cleanup

sections.label: Responsible practice
sections.title: Testing requires authorization and a defined scope.
paragraphs: Security research, penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, account recovery, and administrative troubleshooting should operate under explicit authorization.
Permission should identify the systems, accounts, techniques, timing, and data-handling expectations involved.
Finding a weakness does not authorize exploitation beyond what is necessary to verify and report it.
points: Get authorization before testing systems you do not own
Define scope
Define stop conditions
Minimize collection of real user data
Use test accounts and synthetic data whenever possible
Avoid persistence unless explicitly authorized
Avoid service disruption unless explicitly authorized
Record findings without retaining unnecessary sensitive content
Do not expand scope without approval

sections.label: Responsible disclosure
sections.title: Report vulnerabilities without creating unnecessary harm.
paragraphs: A useful security report explains the affected component, conditions required, impact, evidence, and remediation context without exposing unrelated private information.
The objective is to help the responsible party understand and fix the weakness.
points: Use the owner's documented security contact when available
Provide enough evidence to reproduce the issue safely
Do not publish credentials or personal data
Minimize access to real user information
Do not retain unnecessary copies of sensitive material
Avoid threatening or coercive disclosure practices
Give maintainers a reasonable opportunity to understand and address the issue

sections.label: Security operations
sections.title: Operational security depends on repeatable processes.
paragraphs: Strong security is not a collection of heroic interventions. It is a set of repeatable processes for onboarding, access review, patching, monitoring, incident response, backups, recovery, vendor management, and offboarding.
points: Maintain asset inventories
Maintain account and privilege inventories
Define patching responsibilities
Review critical access periodically
Test backup restoration
Document incident-response contacts
Remove departed users and expired vendor access
Track security exceptions
Review exceptions rather than letting them become permanent

sections.label: Third parties
sections.title: Vendors and integrations extend your security boundary.
paragraphs: Third-party services, contractors, plugins, APIs, SaaS applications, and support providers may have access to sensitive systems or data. Their permissions should be intentionally scoped and periodically reviewed.
points: Grant vendors only the access they require
Use named accounts instead of shared credentials
Set expiration dates for temporary access
Review OAuth and API scopes
Remove unused integrations
Know where sensitive data is transferred
Revoke access after contracts or support engagements end

sections.label: Physical security
sections.title: Cybersecurity still depends on physical control.
paragraphs: A stolen unlocked device, exposed recovery code, unattended administrator workstation, or physically accessible network appliance can bypass otherwise strong digital controls.
points: Lock unattended devices
Protect hardware security keys
Secure network and server equipment
Do not leave recovery codes visible
Dispose of storage media securely
Protect printed sensitive information
Restrict physical access to critical infrastructure

sections.label: Travel and public spaces
sections.title: Security context changes when you leave a trusted environment.
paragraphs: Travel and shared spaces increase the risk of device loss, shoulder surfing, untrusted charging equipment, hostile networks, and unexpected access requests.
points: Minimize sensitive data carried on travel devices
Use screen privacy where appropriate
Avoid leaving devices unattended
Use trusted charging equipment
Keep critical recovery information separate from the primary device
Assume unknown local networks are untrusted

sections.label: Personal information
sections.title: Public information can become authentication material for an attacker.
paragraphs: Birthdays, family relationships, employers, travel dates, schools, addresses, phone numbers, pets, routines, and photographs can help attackers impersonate someone or answer security questions.
points: Review what your public profiles reveal
Limit unnecessary location sharing
Avoid using publicly discoverable information as recovery answers
Be cautious with public travel announcements
Review old posts as well as new ones
Remember that deleted public information may already have been copied

sections.label: Security awareness
sections.title: Awareness should create useful habits, not fear.
paragraphs: People remember clear routines better than long lists of abstract warnings. Awareness should teach what suspicious behavior looks like, how to verify it, where to report it, and what happens after a mistake.
Blaming people for being deceived discourages reporting. Faster reporting usually gives defenders more options.
points: Make reporting simple
Avoid punishing honest reporting
Teach verification habits
Use examples relevant to the person's environment
Explain why controls exist
Practice recovery as well as prevention
Measure whether people can complete secure workflows successfully

sections.label: Human-centered design
sections.title: Secure systems should not depend on perfect human behavior.
paragraphs: People make mistakes under pressure, distraction, fatigue, urgency, and unfamiliarity. Security architecture should assume normal human error and limit the damage a single mistake can cause.
Warnings should be specific and actionable. Recovery should be possible without bypassing security. Important protections should be enabled by default.
points: Make the secure path the easiest normal path
Reduce unnecessary prompts
Avoid repeated security decisions that create alert fatigue
Use clear language
Design safe recovery
Treat confusion and interruption as security costs

sections.label: Professional conduct
sections.title: Security expertise should be paired with restraint.
paragraphs: A security specialist may be capable of bypassing weak privacy settings, examining exposed data, or obtaining access that an ordinary user cannot. Professionalism is demonstrated by choosing not to exceed the legitimate purpose.
The goal is not to prove that access is possible. The goal is to reduce risk with the least unnecessary intrusion.
points: Access only what is necessary
Do not browse unrelated private content
Do not retain copies without a legitimate need
Do not impersonate the account owner
Do not use credentials outside the approved task
Record significant changes when working professionally
Return control to the owner when the work is finished
Remove temporary privileges and credentials

sections.label: Boundaries
sections.title: Helping someone with security still requires respect for their autonomy.
paragraphs: Concern for another person's safety can justify warning them, explaining a risk, helping them review settings, or assisting with recovery when they ask.
It does not automatically justify entering their account, reading private content, changing settings, installing software, tracking them, or impersonating them.
A security specialist should be able to explain what access is needed, why it is needed, what will be changed, what information may become visible during the work, and when that access will end.
sections.callout: Protecting someone and respecting their privacy are the same security objective, not competing ones.

sections.label: Daily practice
sections.title: A practical personal security baseline.
points: Use unique passwords
Use a password manager
Enable strong MFA or passkeys
Secure your primary email
Secure recovery methods
Keep devices updated
Keep applications updated
Review active sessions
Review connected applications
Remove stale devices
Limit public personal information
Verify unexpected requests through another channel
Back up important data
Test recovery procedures
Use standard accounts for daily work
Separate privileged accounts
Revoke access you no longer need
Report suspicious activity early
Never interpret technical capability as permission

sections.label: Privileged checklist
sections.title: A practical privileged-access baseline.
points: Identify every privileged account
Assign each account to an accountable owner
Require strong MFA
Separate administrative and daily-use identities
Eliminate shared credentials where possible
Use least privilege
Use time-limited privilege where practical
Monitor privileged sign-ins
Log significant administrative actions
Review privilege regularly
Protect emergency accounts
Review service-account permissions
Rotate credentials after exposure or personnel changes
Revoke contractor and vendor access when work ends
Never use administrator access to browse unrelated private data

sections.label: Incident checklist
sections.title: A practical compromise-response baseline.
points: Use a trusted device
Secure the primary email account
Change exposed credentials
Revoke active sessions
Review MFA methods
Review recovery methods
Review connected applications
Remove suspicious tokens and keys
Check email forwarding and filters
Review administrator and privileged users
Inspect affected devices for compromise
Preserve relevant evidence
Notify affected parties
Document the timeline
Verify that persistence has been removed

sections.label: Core lesson
sections.title: Capability, access, authorization, and trust are not the same thing.
paragraphs: Capability means you know how to do something.
Access means a system technically allows you to do it.
Authorization means you are permitted to do it.
Trust means someone expects you to use that capability and access within agreed boundaries.
Security professionalism requires understanding the difference.

sections.label: Closing
sections.title: The strongest security preserves both safety and dignity.
paragraphs: Security is not demonstrated by how much access a person can obtain. It is demonstrated by how carefully access is constrained, how little private data needs to be touched, how reliably people can stay safe, and how well systems recover when something goes wrong.
Knowledge should reduce another person's risk without turning them into a subject of unnecessary surveillance.
Good security protects accounts, systems, data, privacy, autonomy, and trust at the same time.
